$comment: Parameter file for the Florida harvester ant. Every value carries a `tag` of A (documented for P. badius), B (generalised from another species) or C (invented, tuned for playability). Values tagged C are the ONLY ones free to change for feel. See docs/SCIENCE.md.

species.habitat: Longleaf pine sandhills, Apalachicola National Forest, north Florida

queens.note: Monogynous. Mature wild colonies never truly polygynous.

maxWorkers.note: Kwapich and Tschinkel 2013. Colonies sampled ran from 157 to 9656 adults.

activeMonths.note: In northern Florida colonies are active between March and November.

daysFirstForagingToLarvae.note: Table 1 of Kwapich and Tschinkel 2013. Foragers precede larvae by 30 to 40 days.

majorWorkerFraction.note: Independent of colony size; rises slightly midsummer.

minorWorkerDryMassMg.note: Dark minor worker, annual mean. Read from Figure 5 of Tschinkel 1998 (plotted 0.6-power transformed; back-transformed here). Cycles from about 2.75 mg in July to 3.45 mg in January, the 24 percent gain the text reports. Replaces an earlier estimate of 1.7 mg, which was wrong by nearly a factor of two and had been feeding the excavation rate.

minorWorkerLeanMassMg.note: Figure 8 of Tschinkel 1998, back-transformed. Varies far less than dry weight: most of the seasonal weight change is fat, not tissue.

majorWorkerDryMassMg.note: ESTIMATE. Tschinkel 1998 reports major dry weights as more variable and subject to sampling error, and does not give a clean annual mean. Scaled from the minor by the cube of the headwidth ratio.

minorHeadwidthInterceptMm.note: Minor worker headwidth = 0.23 log10(workers) + 0.994. R2 = 0.64. Minors grow as the colony grows: 1.15 mm in incipient colonies, 1.90 mm at seven to eight thousand workers.

majorHeadwidthMm.note: HARD RULE that this does NOT scale with colony size: major headwidth showed no significant relationship to worker number. Minors grow as the colony grows; majors do not. Maximum 2.75 mm in July, minimum 2.50 mm in January.

queenLengthMm.note: Body length of the queen, from a secondary account: the UF/IFAS extension sheet on the species (EDIS EENY-298), which does not give its own source. No primary measurement of queen length was found. Used only to draw her; her head width, below, is primary.

queenHeadwidthMm.note: Gyne head width, SD 0.2. Table 1 of Smith and Tschinkel 2006. Gyne size does not change with colony size.

maleHeadwidthMm.note: SD 0.15. Table 1 of Smith and Tschinkel 2006. Larger colonies produce larger males. No male body length was found, so a male is drawn at the queen's length scaled by the ratio of their head widths, and the legend says so.

firstMajorAppearsAtWorkers.note: Solution of the major-number regression. Very small colonies have no majors at all.

majorWorkerFractionBySeason.note: By month, from the May, July, October and January samples of Tschinkel 1998. The annual mean is 7.4 percent (SD 4.5); the midsummer rise the summary mentions is the July figure of 10.6 percent.

queenLifespanYears.note: INVENTED. No lifespan constant appears in the cited literature, but v1 requires colony death. Applied as a per-day hazard, not a hard cap. Exposed as a slider. See docs/DECISIONS.md D4.

nest.$comment: Rewritten from docs/papers/tschinkel-2004-nest-architecture.pdf, read in full. 33 excavations and casts, 2 to 3.02 m deep, 5 to 150 chambers. Size classes: 0 under 100 workers, 1 is 101-800, 2 is 801-2000, 3 is 2001-4000, 4 is over 4000.

incipientDepthCm.note: CORRECTED from 40-50, which came from a secondary account. Tschinkel 2004 measured 29 to 37 cm.

meanDepthAcrossColoniesCm.note: SD 54.2, range 40 to 270 cm, across 42 nests of all sizes (Kwapich and Tschinkel 2013). The 250-300 cm figure is a mature nest, not an average one.

surfaceDiscDiameterCm.note: The very slight, flattened mound of excavated sand around the entrance, often covered with small pebbles or charcoal. From a secondary account, the UF/IFAS extension sheet (EDIS EENY-298), citing Smith and Whitman 1992. Drawn only; the model does not build the disc.

shaftHelixDiameterCm.note: Diameter of the spiral, not of the shaft bore.

shaftBoreDiameterCm.note: A little under 1 cm, near-constant with nest size.

shaftBoreDiameterUpperNestCm.note: Upper nest shafts are larger and flattened-oval, up to about 2 cm wide.

helixPitchShallowCm.note: Shaft length per turn near the surface. Sets the projected zigzag in the vertical slice.

helixLeftHandedBias.note: Tschinkel 2004 says shafts spiral more often left than right but gives no ratio. Bias invented.

shaftAngleDegShallow.note: CORRECTED. From the body of Tschinkel 2004. The abstract of the same paper says 15-20 degrees; the two disagree and the body is used. See docs/SCIENCE.md section 2.

shaftAngleDegDeep.note: CORRECTED. Body text, reached by about 50 cm. The abstract says about 70 degrees.

shaftAngleDegAbstractShallow.note: The abstract's figures, kept so the internal inconsistency in the source stays visible rather than being silently resolved.

chamberAreaDecayPerDepthDecile.note: SUPERSEDED by chamberAreaDecreaseSlope and Intercept below, which are the regression this range summarises. Kept because it is what the abstract of Tschinkel 2004 says. See docs/DECISIONS.md D5.

chamberAreaDecreaseSlope.note: Proportional decrease from one decile to the next is 0.10 * decile - 0.12, rising from about 10 percent between deciles 1 and 2 to about 90 percent between 9 and 10. This is the real relationship; the flat 25-40 percent is a summary of it.

decileAreaDepthLogSlope.note: Log-log slope of decile area against mean decile depth, the same for every colony size class. A tenfold depth increase gives a 75 percent area decrease.

topQuarterAreaFraction.note: About half the total chamber area lies in the top quarter of the nest.

chamberAreaSurfaceToBottomRatio.note: Mean chamber area near the surface relative to near the bottom.

chamberPerimeterRatioSmall.note: Actual perimeter over the perimeter of a circle of equal area. Small chambers are circular.

chamberPerimeterRatioLargeUpper.note: Large chambers of the upper third are strongly lobed.

verticalSpacingDeepCm.note: From the body text of Tschinkel 2004. SUPERSEDED by verticalSpacingByDecileCm below, which is read off Figure 10 of the same paper and peaks near 12 cm, not 20-30. The text appears to quote the class-2 outlier nest. Kept so the disagreement stays visible.

verticalSpacingByDecileCm.note: Read from Figure 10 of Tschinkel 2004: depth increments between chambers, by decile, pooled across size classes. Rises to a maximum in the 7th or 8th decile then decreases again. This is the measured relationship; verticalSpacingDeepCm is the text's summary of it and overstates the maximum.

meanChamberAreaShallowCm2.note: Figure 9B of Tschinkel 2004, uppermost deciles of the larger size classes.

meanChamberAreaDeepCm2.note: Figure 9B, deepest deciles. The 5 to 6 fold surface-to-bottom ratio in the text follows from these two.

chambersPerDecileShallow.note: Figure 9A, uppermost decile, largest size class.

maxVerticalSpacingDecile.note: Spacing peaks here and decreases again in the 10th decile.

superficialChamberMaxDepthCm.note: Within 10 to 15 cm. Modified shafts, lobed on both sides, looping and interconnected in large nests.

shaftBranchingMaxDepthCm.note: Every branch begins above this, whatever the nest size.

workersPerSeries.note: Mean worker number for nests with 1, 2, 3 and 4 vertical series.

areaPerChamberBySeriesCm2.note: Mean area each chamber adds, by series index. Later series contribute less.

totalAreaLogIntercept.note: log10(total chamber area cm2) = 0.551 + 0.873 * log10(dark workers). R2 = 93 percent.

maxDepthLogIntercept.note: log10(max depth cm) = 0.95 + 0.37 * log10(dark workers). R2 = 72 percent.

topDecileAreaByClassCm2.note: Mean area of the uppermost decile, size classes 0 to 4.

colonySizeClassBounds.note: Upper bounds of size classes 0 to 3; class 4 is above the last.

relocationExcavationDays.note: To 2 m and 8 L; most progress in the first days (Tschinkel and Seal 2015). Distinct from wholeNestExcavationDays below, which is the rate a colony can build at when it starts fresh.

wholeNestExcavationDays.note: The workers of a colony can excavate a complete nest in this long, whatever the colony size (Tschinkel 2004). About 5000 workers moved roughly 20 kg of sand in 4 to 5 days.

foundingQueenDepthByDayCm.note: Depth of a founding queen's nest at the end of her first, second and third day of digging. Pogonomyrmex rugosus, fully claustral like badius, in sand-filled frames at 30 C, means of 39 to 42 queens (Enzmann and Nonacs 2010, Table 1). No such series is published for badius. The rugosus queens stopped at 17.11 cm after 7.13 days, but their frames held only 17.75 to 19 cm of soil, so that stopping depth is not used: a badius queen stops at nest.incipientDepthCm.

foundingQueenLateRateCmPerDay.note: The same queens' digging rate between their second and third day, the last interval measured before the frame ran out. Used for a founding queen's shaft after day three, and for her chamber. Enzmann and Nonacs 2010, Table 1.

diggingFatigueSandCm3.note: INVENTED, and fitted. Sand a worker has dug herself, in cubic centimetres, at which her willingness to dig has fallen to about a third. The mechanism is [B]: Rasse and Deneubourg 2001 found that what holds a Lasius niger nest to its population is the nest's volume together with a change in the ants themselves after digging. No such quantity is published for any ant, so this value was fitted to Tschinkel's depth law across colony sizes. See docs/DECISIONS.md D28.

descenderShare.note: INVENTED, and fitted. The share of diggers who walk down to the working face and deepen the shaft; the rest dig where they rest and widen chambers. That digging subsides as a nest grows because the ants spread through it is [B] (Buhl et al. 2005; Halley et al. 2005), and that individuals differ in how they dig is [B] (Rajendran et al. 2025: young Camponotus fellah workers dig slanted tunnels, older ones dig straight down). The share itself is fitted to Tschinkel's depth law. See docs/DECISIONS.md D28.

foundingChamberRunCm.note: INVENTED. Width, in the slice, of the single chamber a founding queen opens at the bottom of her shaft. Small badius chambers are circular and 1 cm high (Tschinkel 2004), but no incipient chamber has been measured. About three queen lengths.

sandPerWorkerPerDayBodyWeights.note: A worker shifts this many times its own weight per day while excavating.

diggingParticipationOld.note: Fraction of workers that actually dig. The difference between age groups is mostly how many dig, not how fast each digs.

diggingIsAPersistentTrait.note: HARD RULE. Tschinkel 2004: a worker either digs consistently or does not dig at all. Digging must be a persistent individual state, never a per-tick coin flip.

superficialChamberChance.note: Chance a dig above superficialChamberMaxDepthCm goes sideways rather than down. Superficial chambers are modified shafts, widened and lobed on both sides (Tschinkel 2004); the strength of that preference is invented.

ceilingRaiseChance.note: Chance a dig is aimed at the ceiling rather than sideways, while the ceiling is still below a body height. Invented.

geotaxisWeight.note: How strongly an unburdened digger heads downward. Gravity is the only reason a colony that starts at the surface reaches three metres. Invented.

digFaceAttraction.note: How strongly an ant is drawn to a cell where there is soil to work. Invented.

walkNoise.note: Randomness in an ant's choice of next cell, so it does not lock onto one gradient. Invented.

crowdAvoidance.note: How strongly an ant avoids a space that already holds nestmates. Set too high the shaft tip admits one ant and the nest takes a simulated year to reach a metre; set to zero the colony packs into ten cells and nothing can dig. Invented, and one of the values tuned against the architectural signature.

relayDistanceCm.note: How far one carrier takes a pellet before putting it down for the next. Staged transport is documented for this species (Tschinkel and Seal 2015) but no leg length is published.

relayPickUpChance.note: Chance an unburdened ant standing on a relay drop takes it on. Below 1 so the colony is not all carriers and no diggers. Invented.

chamberInitiationChance.note: Chance an ant standing on a bare stretch of shaft wall starts a new chamber there, when no chamber lies within the spacing for that depth. This is what opens faces along the whole shaft rather than only at its tip, and without it the colony cannot realise the excavation rate the papers report. Invented.

seriesCountProbeDepthCm.note: Depth at which the validation harness counts separate shaft series. Below shaftBranchingMaxDepthCm so no new branch can start there. A measurement choice, not a behaviour.

pelletsPerExcavatorPerHour.note: Atta vollenweideri. No badius figure published.

digRateSaturationExponent.note: Long-time tunnel growth scales as t^-1/2.

soilMoistureDiggableMax.note: Cannot dig fully dry or fully saturated sand.

buildingPheromoneLifetimeTicks.note: EXPOSED AS A UI SLIDER. Khuong et al. 2016 show this parameter dominates nest form. No badius value exists.

stressSensitivity.note: Digging probability falls as (1 - stress) raised to this power. Ants remove grains under low stress (Buarque de Macedo et al. 2021); the exponent is invented.

spoilCueWeight.note: How strongly accumulated fresh pellets attract the next excavator (Pielstrom and Roces 2013). Strength invented.

collisionAgitationHalfLifeTicks.note: Decay of an ant own recent-collision memory, which is what modulates its digging rate (Avinery et al. 2023). No published value.

crowdingRadiusCm.note: The neighbourhood over which an ant judges how crowded the nest is. A grid cell is 5 mm and a minor worker is 6.35 mm long, so co-occupancy of a single cell is not a collision rate, it is a rounding artefact — and it reports every narrow shaft as crowded.

collisionSaturationCount.note: Local ant density, in ants per void cell, at which digging effort reaches half its maximum. Avinery et al. 2023 find that collisions with nestmates AGITATE ants into digging: a crowded nest is dug out, a roomy one is not. Getting this backwards let six nanitics dig a two-metre nest.

collisionResponseExponent.note: Exponent of the crowding response. Avinery et al. 2023 describe a curve that runs constant, then decays rapidly, then tails off, which suggests a threshold rather than a proportion, and 2.0 was tried. It deadlocks the bootstrap: a colony on the surface has no crowding, so it cannot dig, so it never gets underground to become crowded. Left at 1.0, and the reason is recorded rather than the parameter quietly deleted.

collisionDigBaseline.note: Digging drive in a completely empty neighbourhood. Near zero: a colony with room to spare has no reason to dig, and the founding queen has her own rule.

tunnelLengthFeedbackCm.note: Ants dig less in a tunnel that is already long (Bruce et al. 2018). Length scale invented.

depthCueMechanism.note: HONESTY FLAG. Shaft angle steepens with depth and branching stops below 40 cm, both [A] observations, but no ant knows how deep it is. The CO2-gradient hypothesis was tested by venting and by reversing the gradient and was FALSIFIED (Tschinkel 2013). This simulation gives a digging ant access to its own depth as a stand-in for an unidentified local cue. It is the largest invented element in the excavation model and must be surfaced in the how-do-we-know-this panel. See docs/SCIENCE.md section 11.

surfaceTemperatureDepthGainCmPerC.note: Warmer surface temperatures produce deeper nests (Sankovitz and Purcell 2021). Direction is [B]; this magnitude is invented.

stratificationShallowProbeCm.note: The depth foragerFractionBelow20cm and transferWorkerFractionBelow20cm are measured against. Tschinkel and Kwapich 2017 sorted nests chamber by chamber and reported the fractions below this depth; it is their measurement boundary, not a threshold any ant senses.

stratificationDeepProbeCm.note: The depth broodCareFractionBelow70cm is measured against. Same source and the same caveat.

foragerFatThreshold.note: A worker becomes a forager below this fat fraction. Figure 7B of Tschinkel 1998 gives the context: workers at the surface average about 9 to 10 percent fat, against 28 percent in the bottom third of the nest.

workerFatFractionByDepthThird.note: Surface, then upper, middle and bottom thirds of the nest. Figure 7B of Tschinkel 1998. Fat rises steeply with depth, which is the same gradient as the age gradient: lean workers are at the top because they are old and foraging, not because the top is a hungry place.

workerFatFractionBySeason.note: By month, interpolated between the four samples of Tschinkel 1998: minimum about 19 percent in May and July after sexual production, maximum 25 percent in January. Colony mean across all depths, so well above the 10 percent threshold that marks an individual forager.

ageAtFirstForagingDaysAutumnBorn.note: SUPERSEDED by ageAtFirstForagingDaysAutumnBornRange. Kwapich and Tschinkel 2013 give 210 to 360 days; the youngest winter workers first foraged the following July, eight months after the last eclosion.

ageAtFirstForagingSummerBornSd.note: n = 10 colonies. Strikingly tight for a biological rate.

maxProportionForaging.note: Annual maximum, midsummer, 2009-2012. Foraging begins late February to early April and falls to zero by December.

proportionForagingImmatureMean.note: Colonies under 800 workers reach a higher proportion foraging than mature ones, investing in growth rather than reproduction.

foragersPerLarva.note: SD 0.99. Percent larvae and percent foraging move in parallel, r = 0.759, from May to October.

foragerLeadsLarvaeDays.note: Foragers appear more than a month before the year's first larvae, so larval cues cannot be what stimulates workers to forage.

foragerObservedMaxDepthCm.note: Deepest a marked forager was found in nests sorted chamber by chamber. 96 percent were in the top 20 cm.

midcolouredFractionEarlySpring.note: March. No workers remain in the callow phase.

foragerLifespanDays.note: From first foraging trip, under natural conditions.

taskReversionAllowed.note: HARD RULE. Foragers never revert to inside work.

backfillFromOtherCastes.note: HARD RULE. Removing foragers draws no replacements. Larvae starve instead.

foragingSeasonMonths.note: HARD RULE on the winter end. Foraging begins between late February and early April and falls to zero by December (Kwapich and Tschinkel 2013, Table 1 and Figure 3). A worker whose own schedule comes due in the winter waits for the season; it does not start foraging in January.

foragingOnsetSoilTempC.note: Soil temperature at forager depth below which a worker due to forage holds off. Foraging began within five days of 1 March in three of four study years but a full month later in 2010, so onset is clearly temperature-driven rather than calendar-driven. The threshold itself is not published.

foragingOnsetTempSpanC.note: Degrees above the threshold at which the daily chance of taking up foraging saturates. This is what spreads the overwintered backlog across the spring instead of releasing it all on one day, which produced a March spike and an April trough in a species whose foraging rises steadily from March to a midsummer maximum.

winterWorkerMortalityPerDay.note: INVENTED rate, but the pattern is [A]: spring's rise in proportion foraging is driven by an increase in forager number together with a REDUCTION in colony size, so the colony must lose workers over the winter. Tuned so that a mature colony enters spring smaller than it entered winter.

autumnWorkerWeightGain.note: Fat stored for overwintering and next year's alates.

trunkTrailCount.note: Short trunk trails into a surrounding range.

siteFidelityRadiusMetres.note: P. barbatus. Forager returns to within this of its last site.

rangeActivelyDefended.note: Ranges are exclusive in practice but not defended.

workerSizePredictsSeedSize.note: HARD RULE. Tested and rejected (Ferster & Traniello 1995).

maxOpenableSeedWidthMm.note: Maximum width a worker can OPEN. Wider seeds are still collected and stored; see seeds.largeSeedStoreFractionByWeight and docs/DECISIONS.md D2.

speedMetresPerTick.note: About 5 cm/s, which is the right order for a harvester ant but is not taken from a measurement of this species. A tick is one simulated minute. Chosen so that the walking part of a trip to the far edge of the range takes about seven minutes, leaving trip duration dominated by search time, which is what Beverly et al. found.

maxTripTicks.note: Minutes a forager will search before giving up and coming home empty. No published value; a budget, not a biological constant.

departureChancePerTick.note: Per-tick chance that a forager already indoors and off duty starts a trip. Sets how much of the foraging force is out at once, not who forages: that is fixed by the one-way age progression and nothing here may alter it.

encounterChancePerTick.note: Chance of noticing a seed in the cell the ant is standing in. Search is imperfect; without this the first ant into a patch strips it.

searchTurnSdTurns.note: Standard deviation of the random turn taken each step while searching. Sets how straight an outbound path is.

trunkTrailAngularSpreadTurns.note: How widely departures fan out around a trunk trail direction.

trunkTrailJitter.note: How irregularly the trunk trails are spaced around the compass, as a fraction of even spacing. Zero would space them with a regularity no colony has.

trailSensingDistanceM.note: How far ahead the ant samples trail strength to either side. A nose length, not a survey: an ant with two antennae can compare left with right and nothing more.

trailSensingTurns.note: Angle either side of its heading at which the ant samples.

trailFollowingStrength.note: How hard a trail difference pulls the heading round, in turns. Deliberately of the same order as the search turn noise: a trail that captured every forager the moment it existed would never be tested against the alternatives, and the winner-take-all behaviour reported for this species is a property of the non-linear response, not of an irresistible attraction.

recruitmentDepositPerStep.note: Units of recruitment pheromone laid per step on a laden return leg. No published value exists for badius; the scale is arbitrary and only ratios matter.

seedPatchCount.note: Seeds on the ground are not spread evenly and a model in which they are has no searching in it: every ant finds a seed within a few steps of the entrance, every trip succeeds, and site fidelity and recruitment trails are decorations on a conveyor belt. Patches give search a cost and therefore give memory and recruitment something to be worth. No seed distribution is published for these sandhills; the count and the radius are invented.

seedPatchRadiusM.note: Radius of a patch. Comfortably larger than the half-metre a forager returns to, so a remembered site lands the ant back inside the patch it found.

backgroundSeedsPerSquareMetre.note: Scattered seeds away from any patch. Not zero, so that a wandering ant is occasionally rewarded and the colony is not wholly dependent on the patches it happens to have found.

standingSeedsPerSquareMetre.note: Standing crop of harvestable seeds. No seed rain is published for these sandhills. Tuned against the observation that a range is used almost exclusively by one colony and is not exhausted by it.

seedReplenishmentPerDay.note: Fraction of the shortfall to the standing crop that returns each day. Invented.

surfaceTemperatureMaxC.note: Surface temperature above which foraging stops. That harvester ants have such a limit is well supported in the desert Pogonomyrmex water-loss literature [B]; no threshold is published for badius, so the number itself is invented and exposed as a slider.

activeDayFractionStart.note: Foraging starts about 06:00. These are diurnal ants; the hours are invented.

maxCollectableSeedWidthMm.note: Maximum width a worker can carry home. No published value. Tuned so that large seeds reach the observed 70% of stores by weight.

brood.$comment: Stage durations are not published for P. badius. They are bracketed by Table 1 of Kwapich and Tschinkel 2013, which gives the interval from a colony's first foraging to the appearance of larvae, of pupae and of callow workers, and are tagged B accordingly.

eggDurationDays.note: No badius figure. Bracketed by the 30 to 44 days between first foraging and the appearance of larvae.

larvaDurationDays.note: Bracketed by the interval between larvae and pupae appearing.

pupaDurationDays.note: Bracketed by the interval between pupae and callow workers appearing.

callowDurationDays.note: Time spent pale and non-working after eclosion.

eggVolumeNl.note: Volume of a viable egg of Pogonomyrmex rugosus, SE 1.6, n = 14 (Genzoni et al. 2025). No egg size is published for badius. Used only to draw eggs.

eggLengthToWidth.note: INVENTED. Ant eggs are ovoid, but this ratio is not a measurement. With the volume above it draws an egg about 0.68 mm long and 0.42 mm wide.

matureLarvaLengthToMinorWorker.note: INVENTED. No larval length was found for badius or a close relative; Wheeler and Wheeler 1952 describe Pogonomyrmex larvae but could not be obtained. A fully fed larva is drawn at this fraction of a minor worker's length, and younger larvae smaller.

pupaLengthToAdult.note: A worker pupa already has the adult body plan, with legs and antennae folded against it, so it is drawn at the length of the worker it will become. The equality is an assumption, not a measurement.

noOverwinteringBrood.note: HARD RULE. P. badius colonies do not overwinter with brood; October is the latest possible date of pupal eclosion. Larvae still present after that are doomed and were observed as such.

queenEggsPerDayMature.note: INVENTED. No laying rate is published for this species. Tuned so a colony reaches the 700 workers of sexual maturity in the 4 to 5 years Pogonomyrmex colonies are reported to take, and a mean mature size near 4300.

queenEggsPerDayFounding.note: INVENTED. A claustral queen laying from her own reserves.

nanaticsForageImmediately.note: The first, undersized workers open the nest and begin foraging at once rather than waiting out the age schedule their later sisters follow. General to claustral ants; no badius timing published.

starvationForagerRatioTolerance.note: Larvae begin to starve when foragers fall below this fraction of the observed 1.64 foragers per larva. That ratio is a correlation in mature colonies, not a feeding requirement, and using it as a hard threshold starves every founding colony. A real food account arrives with the seed store at step 7; until then this is a backstop.

alateShareBalanced.note: Share of spring eggs destined to be sexuals under the player's balanced setting. Invented; the lever biases developmental scheduling only and can never reassign an adult.

alateBroodMonths.note: Brood that becomes the June alates is laid in the preceding spring, paid for out of worker fat stored the previous autumn. Months inferred from the flight date and stage durations; not directly published.

eclosionDepthBand.note: New adults are spread through the deepest third of the nest. Callows occur in the bottom third [A]; the spread within it is invented.

transferFractionOfForagingAge.note: How far through its journey to foraging a worker becomes a transfer worker. Invented; the progression itself and its one-way direction are [A].

insideWorkerLifespanDays.note: INVENTED. No inside-worker lifespan is published for this species; only the forager's 27 days is.

autumnFatGainMonths.note: Workers gain about 24 percent in weight across the autumn, storing fat for overwintering and next year's alates.

queenEggsPerWorkerPerDay.note: INVENTED. Laying is limited by how much brood the workers can feed, so it scales with worker number up to the mature rate. Tuned so a colony reaches the 700 workers of sexual maturity in about the 4 to 5 years Pogonomyrmex colonies are reported to take.

nanaticCount.note: Undersized first workers raised entirely from the queen's fat and flight muscle. General to claustral ants; no badius count published.

queenFoundingFatReserve.note: Fraction of the queen's starting reserve. Founding fails if it reaches zero before the first workers eclose.

interior.$comment: How an ant that is not digging moves around inside the nest, and how brood and seeds get where they are kept. WHERE each group ends up is [A] — Tschinkel and Kwapich 2017 sorted whole nests chamber by chamber and counted. HOW an ant gets there is invented: no one has watched a badius worker choose a chamber, and an ant walking toward a depth is the same admitted fiction as the depth cue in excavation. See docs/SCIENCE.md sections 4 and 11.

stepIntervalTicks.note: INVENTED. An ant inside the nest is considered for a step every this many ticks, staggered across the population so they do not all move on the same tick. A tick is a simulated minute and a cell is 5 mm, so this is far slower than an ant walks; what the model takes from this movement is the DISTRIBUTION of ants through the nest, which is measured, and not their speed, which is not. It is also the cost control: the alternative is an eight-neighbour scan for every ant on every tick of every simulated year.

depthPreferenceWeight.note: INVENTED. How strongly a step toward the ant's own preferred depth is favoured over one away from it. This is the term that produces the measured stratification, and it is a fiction: no ant knows its depth. See docs/SCIENCE.md section 11.

walkNoise.note: INVENTED. Random weight added to each candidate step, so that ants at their preferred depth mill about rather than freezing on one cell.

crowdAvoidance.note: INVENTED. Penalty per nestmate already in a candidate cell. Without it a whole nursery stacks on the single deepest cell.

preferredDepthRedrawDays.note: INVENTED. How often an ant redraws its preferred depth from the distribution for its task. Redrawing every tick makes the population distribution right and every individual jittery; never redrawing freezes each ant on one shelf for life.

tendingAttraction.note: INVENTED. How strongly a worker prefers a step onto a cell holding the thing it tends — brood for a brood-care worker, seeds for a transfer worker. Ants gather on what they are working on; without this term a worker walks to its preferred depth and never encounters the pile it is supposed to be moving.

broodPickUpChancePerTick.note: INVENTED. Chance a brood-care worker standing on brood that is shallower than where brood belongs picks a piece up to carry it deeper.

maxBroodPerCell.note: INVENTED. Brood spreads across the floor of a chamber rather than stacking on one cell. A packing limit, not a biological capacity.

broodSearchRadiusCm.note: INVENTED, and a search bound rather than a biological length. How far around the queen a clutch of eggs may be spread while looking for chamber floor to put it on before it settles for whatever void is nearest. Large enough to reach the chambers a queen sits between, small enough that a clutch is a clutch and not a smear down the nest.

broodChamberDepthFraction.note: INVENTED. Brood is carried below this fraction of the nest's current depth. Expressed as a fraction rather than a depth because a founding nest is 30 cm deep and a mature one is three metres, and the brood is deep in both. The pattern it reproduces is [A]: below 70 cm, 90 percent of workers are brood-care workers, and callows eclose in the bottom chambers.

foragerDepositMaxDepthCm.note: INVENTED depth for an [A] behaviour. Tschinkel and Seal 2015 established that foragers deposit seeds only in the topmost chambers and that a separate group carries them down; no one published where 'topmost' stops. A returning forager drops its seed in the first chamber it meets above this depth.

downwardTransportChancePerTick.note: INVENTED. Chance a worker that comes across a seed lying above the seed-chamber band picks it up to take it deeper. High, because the alternative reading — that a worker mostly walks past misplaced food — leaves the whole crop sitting in the entrance: at any moment only a couple of workers are in the top 20 cm, so an opportunity missed is an opportunity that does not come round again for hours. Sets how fast the wave of seeds moves down, which Tschinkel and Seal 2015 describe qualitatively and did not time.

storeBandFractionOfDepth.note: INVENTED. The measured seed chambers sit at 20 to 80 cm, which is deeper than a young colony's whole nest. While the nest is shallower than the band, the store sits below this fraction of whatever depth has been dug. A mature nest never uses this: the measured band applies.

maxSeedsPerCell.note: INVENTED packing limit, so a store spreads across a chamber floor instead of becoming an infinitely deep pile in one cell.

largeSeedStoreFractionByWeight.note: Large seeds accumulate because workers cannot open them.

destinationConstrainedToTrunkTrail.note: Moves always occur along a foraging trail, usually the main one.

causeKnown.note: Surface this in the UI. Cause remains unexplained.

candidateSitesDiffer.note: DELIBERATE DEPARTURE FROM [A]. Tschinkel 2013, 2014 tested soil, architecture, canopy and neighbour density as explanations for relocation and found none; the replacement nest is statistically indistinguishable from the vacated one. This simulator nevertheless gives candidate sites real differences so the player's choice has consequences. Surfaced as invented wherever shown. See docs/DECISIONS.md D3.

pheromones.$comment: No decay or deposition constants are published for P. badius. All numeric values here are tag C and must be exposed as sliders.

building.note: Decay is DERIVED from excavation.buildingPheromoneLifetimeTicks, which is the authored value and the exposed slider. See docs/DECISIONS.md D6.

diffusionIntervalTicks.note: Diffusion is applied on this fixed sub-schedule rather than every tick. Identical at every playback speed and headless, so it does not affect reproducibility. Performance decision; see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

foragersUsePathIntegration.note: Ants hold a homing vector; they do not navigate by trail alone.

time.$comment: Neither SCIENCE.md nor the build brief states a tick length, yet every decayPerTick and ...Ticks value depends on one. See docs/DECISIONS.md D7.

secondsPerTick.note: One simulated minute per tick. 1440 ticks per day, 525600 per year.

soil.$comment: No soil physics values are published for P. badius nests. The thermal model is derived from climate.soilThermalLagDaysPerMetre; the hydrology and stress values below are invented and exposed as sliders.

bulkDensityKgPerM3.note: Dry well-drained sand. Sets the overburden stress profile.

surfaceTemperatureOffsetC.note: Bare sandhill sand runs warmer than screen air temperature. Invented.

infiltrationDepthCmPerMm.note: Depth of sand wetted per mm of rain, given the low water-holding capacity of sand.

deepMoisture.note: Stable moisture below the evaporation zone. Sits inside the diggable window, which is why deep excavation is not rain-gated.

evaporationDepthCm.note: Drying falls off exponentially with this scale, so only shallow soil responds to a dry spell.

archingStressGainPerVoid.note: How much a void raises stress in the soil beside and above it. This is what makes force chains arch over a tunnel; no ant senses the network.

stressShieldBelowFactor.note: Soil directly beneath a void is shielded from overburden, so digging downward stays easier than digging sideways.

discretisation.$comment: NOT BIOLOGY. How the continuous world is chopped into cells. Tagged C because every value here is a modelling choice with no evidential basis, and each is exposed so a user can raise fidelity at the cost of speed. See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

nestCellSizeCm.note: A 1 cm chamber is two cells tall, so chamber height stays measurable rather than true by construction.

nestDepthCm.note: Comfortably past the 250-300 cm mature depth, so the floor of the grid never constrains the nest.

surfaceExtentM.note: Half-width. Covers the 20 m foraging range with margin.

sliceThicknessCm.note: The out-of-plane depth a slice cell stands for, taken as the shaft bore. A vertical slice has no third dimension, but a volume of sand has to be attributed to a cell somewhere or excavation rates in cm3 per worker-day cannot be used at all. Chambers are wider than this out of plane, so cell volume is understated for chambers and about right for shafts. See docs/DECISIONS.md D11.

pheromoneHaloCells.note: Pheromone decay and diffusion are applied only within the excavated region grown by this many cells, and cells beyond it are held at zero. Diffusion carries signal one cell per application and the per-application decay is far below one, so the concentration six cells outside anything ever dug is smaller than a float32 can usefully hold. Raising it costs speed and changes nothing measurable. Performance decision; see docs/DECISIONS.md D19.

climate.$comment: 1991-2020 US climate normals, Tallahassee, Florida. Tag A as a factual record of the study site.

soilThermalLagDaysPerMetre.note: Approximate. Damped, lagged sinusoid with depth.

nuptialFlightTrigger.value: calm humid morning following heavy rain

meanRainEventMm.note: Monthly normals give totals, not events. Rain days are drawn so the expected monthly total matches the table.

heavyRainMm.note: Threshold for the rain that triggers a nuptial flight and that halts excavation by saturation.

events.$comment: v2. Kept here so the v1 schema does not have to change.
